tools.name: search_guidelines
tools.description:
Look a rule up in the UMR guidelines (umr4nlp/umr-guidelines, guidelines.md).

keywords: terms to look for, e.g. "aspect", "modal strength", "have-rel-role-92", ":quant",
"reentrancy". Passages with more of the keywords come first, then those whose heading has
them, then those that mention them most.
max_results: how many passages to return (at most 10).

Returns {"sections": [{"heading": the passage's place in the guidelines ("Part 3. ... > Part
3-3-1. Aspect"), "text": the passage (a section, or a part of a long one)}], "found": how
many passages matched}.

tools.name: propbank_lookup
tools.description:
Look up a lemma and every alternate of it in PropBank (at most 20 per call).

language is "en" or "zh". Returns Markdown: per lemma, every roleset with its roles and all
its examples (the sentence, then each argument; traces such as *T*-1 are PropBank's own),
or "not in PropBank". Lemmas over the limit are not looked up: the last line names them
(call again with them). There is no PropBank for another language (Uzbek): nothing.

tools.name: search_annotations
tools.description:
Find how a case is annotated: gold UMR annotations of whole sentences.

language: "zh" (Chinese) or "en" (English).
keywords: words or pieces to look for, matched anywhere in a sentence or its annotation:
words of the text (e.g. "发生", "wanted to"), concepts ("have-org-role-91", "identity-91"),
roles (":ARG1-of", ":manner"), attribute values (":aspect state"). Sentences with more of the
keywords come first.
max_results: how many gold sentences to return (at most 10).

Returns {"gold": [{"doc", "sentence_number", "sentence", "annotation"}], where annotation is
the sentence's whole annotation (words, sentence-level graph, alignment, document-level
annotation); "found": how many gold sentences matched in all}.

## Input

Language: en
Document: en-0008, sentence 5 of 9

The sentence: its number, a tab, then its words separated by spaces.

5	Pope was flown to the U.S. military base at Ramstein , Germany .

content.content:
## fly

### fly-01 (fly through the air, travel via air, fly in a flock)

- ARG0: pilot, agentive entity capable of flight (like a bird)
- ARG1: passenger, cargo
- ARG2: aircraft flown, flight number, steed, non-agentive thing in motion
- ARG3: type of flight plan, mission, cognate object (like 'a flight' or 'sorties')
- ARG4: airline

Example 1 (fly-v: unaccusative, traveller as subject): And some investors fault Mr. Spiegel's life style; he earns millions of dollars a year and flies around in Columbia's jet planes.
- ARG1: he
- ARGM-DIR: around
- ARG2: in Columbia's jet planes
- rel: flies

Example 2 (fly-v: transitive, pilot as subject): As a ``good-will measure,'' [the pilots]-1 had been working four extra hours a month and had agreed *trace*-1 to fly UAL's two new Boeing 747-400 aircraft.
- ARG0: *trace*-1
- ARG2: UAL's two new Boeing 747-400 aircraft
- rel: fly

Example 3 (fly-v: with destination): He will fly to San Francisco on the afternoon of the 20th to participate in another round of speeches .
- ARG1: He
- ARGM-MOD: will
- ARGM-GOL: to San Francisco
- ARGM-TMP: on the afternoon of the 20th
- ARGM-PRP: to participate in another round of talks
- rel: fly

Example 4 (fly-v: with recipient): John flew the paper airplane to Mary.
- ARG0: John
- ARG2: the paper airplane
- ARGM-GOL: to Mary
- rel: flew

Example 5 (fly-v: with employing airline, arg4): [All of the first group of pilots who went abroad to receive training for new fighter aircraft]-1 have left the military *trace*-1 to fly for civilian airlines
- ARG0: *trace*-1
- ARG4: for civilian airlines
- rel: to fly

Example 6 (fly-v: with arg3): Since this war began, something like 23,000 coalition sorties have been flown.
- ARGM-TMP: Since this war began
- ARG3: something like 23,000 coalition sorties
- rel: flown

Example 7 (flight-n: Within LVC): Just last week , for example , Trans World Airlines and Pan Am Corp. 's Pan American World Airways went so far as to offer cash rebates or gift checks of $ 200 to $ 1,000 to certain frequent-flier members making trans-Atlantic flights in business class or first class .
- ARG1: certain frequent-flier members
- ARGM-LVB: making
- ARGM-DIR: trans-Atlantic
- ARGM-MNR: in business class or first class.
- rel: flights

Example 8 (flight-n: pilot as subject, source and destination): This month we celebrate and remember Amelia Earhart's flight from Hawaii to California.
- ARG0: Amelia Earhart's
- ARGM-DIR: from Hawaii
- ARGM-GOL: to California
- rel: flight

Example 9 (flight-v: With DIR): The maximum count of birds flighting in at dusk was a remarkable 183.
- ARG0: birds
- ARGM-DIR: in
- ARGM-TMP: at dusk
- rel: flighting

Example 10 (fly-v): I never fly Frontier anymore.
- ARG1: I
- ARGM-NEG: never
- ARG4: Frontier
- ARGM-TMP: anymore
- rel: fly

Example 11 (fly-v): He flew on flight 664 to Albuquerque.
- ARG1: He
- ARG2: on flight 664
- ARGM-GOL: to Albuquerque
- rel: flew

Example 12 (For first/business/economy class, use :manner.): When I fly intercontental, I always fly first class.
- ARG1: I
- ARGM-TMP: always
- ARGM-MNR: first class
- rel: fly

### fly-02 (fly in the face of: flout)

- ARG0: flouter
- ARG1: "in the face of __"

Example 1 (ULA example): There I believe we would decidedly fly in the face of established case law .
- ARG0: we
- ARGM-MOD: would
- ARGM-ADV: decidedly
- ARG1: in the face of established case law
- rel: fly

### fly-03 (hit a fly ball, has strange past participle)

- ARG0: hitter
- ARG1: bases
- ARG2: where player moves to after hitting fly ball

Example 1 (Args 0 & 2): Kemp came closest to a home run in the fourth inning when he flied to very deep right field.
- ARG0: he
- ARG2: to very deep right field
- rel: flied

### fly-06 ((cause to) hold a spatial configuration in the air)

- ARG0: causal agent
- ARG1: thing suspended in the air

Example 1 (fly-v): He flew a flag above his house
- ARG0: He
- ARG1: a flag
- ARGM-LOC: above his house
- rel: flew

### fly-yy (insect (and other non-predicative senses))

- (no roles)

Example 1 (fruit fly): A large number of fruit flies hovered over the rotting bananas.

content.text:
I used fly-01, whose ARG1 is the passenger. Pope is that passenger, and nobody is named as the one who flew him. The node's alignment and the document-level links will be added in the later step.

# ::snt 5
# sentence level graph:
(s5f / fly-01
    :ARG1 (s5p / person
        :name (s5n / name :op1 "Pope"))
    :goal (s5b / base
        :mod (s5m / military)
        :mod (s5c / country
            :wiki "United_States"
            :name (s5n2 / name :op1 "U.S."))
        :place (s5c2 / city
            :wiki "Ramstein-Miesenbach"
            :name (s5n3 / name :op1 "Ramstein")
            :part-of (s5c3 / country
                :wiki "Germany"
                :name (s5n4 / name :op1 "Germany"))))
    :aspect performance)

A few choices in the graph:
- **Destination:** "to the U.S. military base" is `:goal`, following the PropBank example "fly to San Francisco".
- **Pope:** a `person` with the name "Pope". I took the name from the sentence alone; I couldn't see the earlier sentences.
- **Aspect:** `performance`, because the flight is finished and reached its destination.
- **The base:** "military" and "U.S." are both `:mod` on `base`. Ramstein is a `city` placed on the base with `:place`, and it is `:part-of` Germany. No gold example for "military base" or "Ramstein" came up, so the structure of this phrase is my own judgment.
- **Wiki title for Ramstein:** I used "Ramstein-Miesenbach" for the town. "Ramstein_Air_Base" would also be a reasonable choice.
